title: ConfigMaps & Secrets
summary: Externalizing configuration and credentials from container images, the Kubernetes-native way — and where the guarantees actually stop.

slides.markdown:
Baking a database URL or a feature flag into an image means rebuilding and re-pushing the image just to change a setting — and the same image can no longer run in dev, staging, and prod unchanged. **ConfigMaps** and **Secrets** decouple config from the image: the image stays generic, and the environment supplies the values at deploy time.

This is also what makes an image *promotable* — the exact same, already-tested image moves from staging to prod, picking up prod's ConfigMap instead of being rebuilt.

slides.subTitle: Creating and consuming them
slides.markdown:
A ConfigMap is a plain key-value bag. It can be consumed as environment variables or as mounted files — the same data, two delivery mechanisms.

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-config
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: "info"
  app.properties: |
    retries=3
    timeout=30s
```

Consumed via `envFrom: configMapRef` for env vars, or `volumeMounts` + `volumes.configMap` to get `app.properties` as an actual file inside the container — useful when the app expects a config file, not env vars.

slides.subTitle: How they differ from ConfigMaps
slides.markdown:
A Secret has the identical shape and API as a ConfigMap — same `data`, same consumption methods — but it's meant for sensitive values (passwords, tokens, certs). By default that's a weaker guarantee than the name implies: Secret values are **base64-encoded, not encrypted**, in etcd, and anyone who can read the Secret object (or an etcd backup) can trivially decode them.

Kubernetes does layer real protections on top — RBAC restricting who can `get` Secrets, and optional **encryption at rest** for etcd — but neither is on by default in a vanilla cluster.

The delivery method decides whether an update is picked up live.

| Method | Update behavior | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| Env var (`envFrom`) | Frozen at container start — needs a Pod restart to change | Simple values, rarely-changed settings |
| Mounted volume | kubelet updates the file in place within ~minutes, no restart | Config an app is designed to reload/watch |

An app has to actually watch the mounted file (inotify or periodic re-read) to benefit from live updates — mounting alone doesn't make an app hot-reload something it wasn't built to reload.

slides.subTitle: Base64 isn't encryption
slides.markdown:
**The wrong belief:** "it's a Secret, so it's encrypted."

**Why it breaks:** by default, Secret values sit in etcd as **base64**, a reversible encoding, not encryption — `echo <value> | base64 -d` recovers the plaintext instantly. Anyone with `get secrets` RBAC, or a copy of an unencrypted etcd snapshot, has the real value.

**The correct model:** enable **encryption at rest** for the Secrets resource in etcd's config, tighten RBAC so `get`/`list` on Secrets is narrowly scoped, and treat cluster-admin and etcd-backup access as equivalent to "can read every credential in the cluster."

Marking a ConfigMap or Secret `immutable: true` prevents further edits — Kubernetes rejects the update instead of silently changing values every Pod is reading. This protects against accidental drift and cuts API server load, which no longer watches that object for changes.

Common pattern: bake a content hash into the **name** (`app-config-a1b2c3`) and reference that from the Deployment. A config change becomes a *new* object plus a Deployment update — which triggers a rolling restart, so Pods pick up new values.

slides.subTitle: Rotating a DB credential with no downtime
slides.markdown:
Create a new Secret (`db-creds-v2`) with the new password, update the database user side-by-side so both old and new passwords are valid briefly, then update the Deployment to reference `db-creds-v2` — which triggers a rolling restart, so Pods pick up the new credential one at a time while old Pods keep working on the old one.

Once every Pod is on the new Secret, revoke the old password on the database. The overlap window is what makes it zero-downtime: nothing ever has to restart all Pods at once against a credential that's already been cut over.

slides.subTitle: A Pod stuck in ContainerCreating
slides.markdown:
A Deployment is applied and the Pod sits in `ContainerCreating` indefinitely, never crashing, never producing a container log — because there is no container yet. `kubectl describe pod` is the only place this shows up: an Event like `configmap "app-config-v2" not found` or `secret "db-creds" not found`.

This happens constantly after a rename or a namespace mismatch — the Deployment references a ConfigMap/Secret name that doesn't exist in that namespace, often because it was renamed in one manifest but not the other, or applied to the wrong namespace entirely. `kubectl get configmap,secret -n <ns>` confirms what actually exists before chasing the Pod spec.

slides.subTitle: Vault, cloud KMS, and the External Secrets Operator
slides.markdown:
Native Secrets stop at "base64 in etcd" — teams needing real encryption, rotation, and audit logging usually put a dedicated secrets manager (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager) in front of Kubernetes instead of trusting etcd directly.

The common integration is the **External Secrets Operator**: it watches an `ExternalSecret` custom resource, fetches the real value from Vault/KMS on a poll interval, and writes it into a normal Kubernetes Secret that Pods consume exactly as before. Kubernetes-native Secrets become a synced *cache* of the real source of truth, not the source of truth itself — rotation happens in Vault, and the operator propagates it.
